slides.title: Introduction to Scheduling
slides.body:
Terminology
Arrival Time
Time at which the process arrives in the ready queue
Completion Time
Time at which process completes its execution and terminates
slides.notes: Before solving scheduling problems, let's understand important terms. Arrival Time is when a process enters the Ready Queue, making it eligible for execution. Completion Time is the exact time at which the process finishes its execution and terminates.

slides.title: Introduction to Scheduling
slides.body:
Terminology
Burst Time
Time required by a process for CPU execution
Turnaround Time
Total amount of time spent by a process in the system
Turnaround Time = Completion Time – Arrival Time
slides.notes: Next, Burst Time refers to the amount of CPU time a process needs to complete its execution. Another important metric is Turnaround Time, which tells us how long a process spends in the system from arrival until completion. We calculate it by subtracting the Arrival Time from the Completion Time.

slides.title: Introduction to Scheduling
slides.body:
Terminology
Waiting Time
Amount of time spent by a process in the ready queue
Response Time
 Time from process arrival in the ready queue to its first CPU execution
Response Time =  First Start Time – Arrival Time
Waiting Time = Turnaround Time – Burst Time

First-Come First-Served
slides.notes: Now, let's begin with the first CPU scheduling algorithm—First-Come, First-Served, or FCFS. As the name suggests, the process that enters the Ready Queue first gets the CPU first. Since FCFS is a non-preemptive algorithm, once a process starts executing, it continues until it completes, even if other processes arrive in the meantime.

slides.title: First-Come First-Served
slides.body:
Convoy Effect
The convoy effect happens in FCFS when one long (CPU-heavy) process arrives first and holds the CPU while several short processes wait behind it
Because FCFS is non-preemptive, the short jobs can't overtake - they're stuck in a "convoy" behind the slow one
Result: Average waiting time and turnaround time shoot up, and the CPU/devices are used inefficiently
slides.notes: However, FCFS has a major drawback called the Convoy Effect. If a long CPU-intensive process gets the CPU first, all the shorter processes have to wait behind it because FCFS is non-preemptive. This increases the average waiting and turnaround times and also leads to poor utilization of the CPU and I/O devices.

slides.title: First-Come First-Served
slides.body: Convoy Effect
slides.notes: One heavily loaded truck on a single-lane road holds up all the fast cars behind it — everyone moves at the truck's speed.

slides.title: First-Come First-Served
slides.body:
First-Come First-Served
When To Use ?
slides.notes: Finally, FCFS works well in batch systems, where processes are long-running and don't require immediate user interaction. It's also a good choice when most processes have similar burst times because of its simple implementation. However, it's generally avoided in interactive systems since the convoy effect can significantly reduce performance.

slides.title: First-Come First-Served
slides.body:
First-Come First-Served
Not Ideal For
Time-sharing systems
Interactive workloads (poor response time due to the convoy effect)
Situations where short jobs must complete early
slides.notes: On the other hand, FCFS is not a good choice for time-sharing or interactive systems, where quick responses are important. It's also unsuitable when short processes need to finish early, since they may end up waiting behind longer processes due to the convoy effect.

slides.title: Scheduling Algorithms
slides.body: Shortest Job First
slides.notes: Now, let's move on to Shortest Job First, or SJF. In this algorithm, the scheduler selects the process with the smallest CPU burst time from the ready queue and executes it first. You may also come across the names Shortest Process Next (SPN) or Shortest Job Next (SJN)—they all refer to the same scheduling approach.

slides.title: Scheduling Algorithms
slides.body: The Core Idea
slides.notes: Moving on, the idea behind SJF is quite straightforward. Whenever the CPU becomes available, the scheduler checks all the processes in the Ready Queue and selects the one with the shortest burst time. If two processes have the same burst time, the tie is broken using FCFS, so the process that arrived first gets the CPU first.

slides.title: Shortest Job First
slides.body: Why To Use It ?
slides.notes: Now, you might wonder why SJF is preferred. The reason is that it produces the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes. By executing shorter jobs first, they finish quickly, reducing the number of processes waiting in the queue and improving overall system performance.

slides.title: Shortest Job First (Non-Preemptive)
slides.body: When Is It Used?
slides.notes: Moving on, Non-Preemptive SJF is commonly used in batch systems, where burst times are already known or can be estimated. It's also suitable for long-term job scheduling and works particularly well when there's a mix of short and long processes, as it helps minimize the average waiting time.

slides.title: Shortest Job First (Non-Preemptive)
slides.body:
When Not To Use?
Not ideal for
Interactive/time-sharing systems (burst time isn't known in advance)
Systems needing predictable response
Environments with many long processes (starvation risk)
slides.notes: However, Non-Preemptive SJF isn't suitable for every scenario.It's not a good fit for interactive or time-sharing systems, where burst times aren't known in advance and quick responses are expected. It can also lead to starvation, as long processes may keep waiting while shorter ones continue to get scheduled.

slides.body: Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)

slides.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms
slides.body:
SRTF – Preemptive SJF
SRTF is the preemptive form of Shortest Job First (SJF)
The scheduler always chooses the process with the least remaining burst time
If a new process arrives with a shorter remaining time than the current process, the CPU is preempted
Continuously checks remaining times to decide the next CPU allocation
slides.notes: Now, unlike SJF, this algorithm can interrupt a running process whenever a better option becomes available. The operating system keeps comparing the remaining execution times of all ready processes, and if a newly arrived process can finish sooner than the current one, it immediately gets the CPU. That's why SRTF is called the preemptive version of SJF.

slides.title: SRTF – Preemptive SJF
slides.body:
Key Points
Can cause many context switches, increasing overhead
Gives minimum average waiting time among all algorithms
Risk of starvation for long processes
slides.notes: Moving on, one of the biggest strengths of SRTF is that it achieves the lowest average waiting time. However, because processes can be interrupted frequently, it results in more context switches, adding overhead. Also, long-running processes may keep getting postponed, which can lead to starvation.

slides.title: SRTF – Preemptive SJF
slides.body: When To Use?
slides.notes: Moving on, SRTF is best suited for systems where reducing the average waiting time is the primary goal and the CPU burst times can be estimated reasonably well. It also performs well in environments where short processes arrive frequently, allowing them to complete quickly.

slides.title: SRTF – Preemptive SJF
slides.body:
When Not To Use?
Not ideal for
Systems where context-switch overhead is costly (SRTF switches often)
Long-running processes (high starvation risk)
Hard real-time systems needing guaranteed timing
slides.notes: However, SRTF isn't suitable for every system. If context switching is expensive, its frequent preemptions can reduce performance. It's also not ideal for long-running processes because they may experience starvation, and it's generally avoided in hard real-time systems, where execution deadlines must be guaranteed.

slides.title: SJF
slides.body: Key Points
slides.notes: Finally, there's one practical challenge with SJF. The operating system doesn't actually know a process's future CPU burst time. Instead, it predicts the next burst based on the process's past execution pattern, commonly using a technique called exponential averaging.

slides.title: SJF
slides.body:
Key Points
Starvation - a long process may keep getting pushed back indefinitely if shorter jobs keep arriving. (This is later solved using aging.)
Main drawback:
slides.notes: However, SJF has one major limitation—starvation. If short processes keep arriving, a long process may keep waiting without getting CPU time. Later, we'll see how a technique called aging helps overcome this problem.

slides.body: Round Robin (RR)
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the Round Robin Scheduling Algorithm

slides.title: Scheduling Algorithms
slides.body:
Round Robin Scheduling (Preemptive)
A CPU scheduling algorithm that gives each process an equal share of CPU time
Processes are handled in a cyclic (round-robin) order from the ready queue
What is Round Robin?
slides.notes: Now, let's move on to Round Robin Scheduling, a preemptive scheduling algorithm. Instead of allowing one process to run until completion, it gives every process an equal opportunity to use the CPU. The processes are executed one after another in a cyclic order, ensuring that each process gets its turn.

slides.title: Scheduling Algorithms
slides.body:
Round Robin Scheduling (Preemptive)
A fixed time slice assigned to each process
If a process doesn’t finish within the quantum, it is preempted and moved to the end of the queue
Time Quantum
slides.notes: Next, Round Robin works using a time quantum, which is a fixed amount of CPU time assigned to each process. If a process finishes within that time, it exits the CPU. Otherwise, it's preempted and moved to the end of the Ready Queue, allowing the next process to get its turn.

slides.title: Round Robin Scheduling (Preemptive)
slides.body: Key Characteristics
slides.notes: Moving on, Round Robin is considered a fair scheduling algorithm because every process gets a chance to execute. The trade-off is that frequent switching between processes increases context-switching overhead. Also, the algorithm's performance depends heavily on choosing an appropriate time quantum—too small or too large can reduce efficiency.

slides.title: Round Robin Scheduling
slides.body:
Effect of Time Quantum Size
Quantum too large
Each process finishes within its slice, so RR behaves like FCFS - you lose responsiveness and the convoy effect can return
Quantum too small
Too many context switches; the CPU wastes time switching instead of doing useful work, lowering throughput
slides.notes: Finally, the choice of time quantum has a big impact on Round Robin's performance. If it's too large, Round Robin starts behaving like FCFS, reducing responsiveness and even bringing back the convoy effect. On the other hand, if it's too small, the CPU spends too much time performing context switches, which lowers the overall throughput.

slides.title: Round Robin Scheduling
slides.body:
Effect of Time Quantum Size
The trade-off
small quantum = better response time but higher overhead; large quantum = lower overhead but poorer response time
Rule of thumb
the quantum should be slightly larger than a typical CPU burst - a common guideline is that ~80% of CPU bursts should be shorter than the quantum (typical real values: 10–100 ms)
slides.notes: Finally, there's always a trade-off when choosing the time quantum. A smaller value gives faster responses but increases the cost of context switching, while a larger value reduces that overhead but makes the system less responsive. In practice, the quantum is usually set slightly higher than a typical CPU burst, so that most processes—around 80%—finish within a single time slice. Common values range from 10 to 100 milliseconds.

slides.title: Round Robin Scheduling
slides.body: When To Use ?
slides.notes: Moving on, Round Robin is widely used in time-sharing, interactive, and multi-user systems, where many users or processes need CPU time. It's preferred in situations where fairness and quick response are more important than achieving the lowest possible turnaround time.

slides.title: Round Robin Scheduling
slides.body: When Not To Use ?
slides.notes: However, Round Robin isn't the best choice in every situation. It's generally avoided in batch systems, where completing jobs quickly is the main objective. It also performs poorly in systems where context switching is expensive, and when processes have very different burst times, the overall turnaround time can increase.
